vignette: Mai, a 25-year-old South Eastern Asian woman married to her high school sweetheart, has always been meticulous about her work as a Database Administrator at a tech company in Silicon Valley. Her life was marked by routine and stability until the fateful day when her car was hit by a truck on her way home from work. The collision was sudden and violent, leaving Mai with severe physical injuries and emotional trauma. The memory of hearing screeching tires and feeling the impact reverberate through her body is seared into her mind. She still vividly remembers how she struggled to breathe as the airbags deployed, and the disorienting sensation of being trapped in the twisted metal. Since the accident, Mai has experienced a range of distressing symptoms that have significantly disrupted her life. The most potent triggers are hearing names related to vehicles or accidents and engaging in arguments, which remind her of the chaos and uncertainty she felt during the collision. Uncertainty itself is another trigger, as it brings back the overwhelming sense of helplessness she endured. In an attempt to cope with these distressing memories, Mai has developed several avoidance behaviors. She avoids situations that put her body under stress, such as going for walks or engaging in any form of physical exertion. Instead, she spends most of her time sitting at her desk, engrossed in work that she can control and predict. Her social life has also been significantly impacted by her trauma. Mai now avoids seeing friends altogether, fearing that arguments could trigger intense flashbacks and anxiety. This isolation has left her feeling increasingly disconnected from the support system she once relied on. To manage her overwhelming thoughts about the accident, Mai resorts to self-harm as a form of distraction. Cutting herself provides a momentary respite from the intrusive memories and helps her feel more in control. She had come to believe that this was the only way to cope with her intense emotional pain. The negative appraisals she harbors further compound her distress. Mai is convinced that the accident happened because of her own actions-that if she had been driving differently, she might have avoided the collision. This self-blame has led to profound feelings of guilt and mistrust towards others. She frequently thinks about how she could not do more to prevent what happened and wonders why no one came to her aid sooner. Mai's husband has noticed a significant change in her demeanor since the accident. Once vibrant and social, Mai now withdraws into herself, preferring solitude over company. Her work performance has also been affected; she spends long hours at her desk but often struggles to focus on tasks that were once routine. The accumulation of these symptoms and avoidance behaviors eventually took their toll on Mai's mental health. She felt increasingly trapped by her trauma, with no clear path forward. It was during a particularly intense episode when the sound of an argument at work triggered a vivid flashback that she realized she needed help. What frightened her most was the fear of being stuck in this cycle indefinitely, unable to move past the traumatic event and reconnect with those around her. Seeking therapy was not just about addressing her symptoms; it was also about regaining control over her life and finding a way to heal from within. Mai hopes that through therapy, she can rediscover a sense of trust and self-worth, allowing her to live more fully without the constant shadow of trauma hanging over her every moment.
